title: Tomorrow
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The everyday Italian future is the PRESENT plus a time word: Domani vado a Roma, Domani lavoro. The time word carries the tense and nothing on the verb changes — English half-shares this with "I'm going tomorrow", so it is a delta you already own half of.
Italian does have a future tense — andrò, lavorerò — and it is used for predictions and promises rather than for arrangements. It belongs to a later level, and nothing in this module needs it.

andare is irregular and carries the module: vado · vai · va. Going to a place takes a — vado a Roma, vado a casa — and going to DO something takes the same a in front of the plain verb: vado a mangiare.
A time phrase built on prossimo agrees with its noun: la settimana prossima (feminine), il mese prossimo (masculine). It stands at the front or at the end, and needs no preposition in either place.

Some of the commonest verbs bend their stems and are learned one at a time: andare gives vado · vai · va, fare gives faccio · fai · fa, uscire gives esco · esci · esce. The endings are the ordinary ones; it is the stem that moves.
The present keeps doing what M4 taught, one ending per person: prendo · prendi · prende, vedo · vedi · vede.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Tomorrow I-go to Rome" — a present tense doing a future's work

words.note: tomorrow. A plain adverb: it takes no article and no preposition, and it stands at the front or at the end. It is what turns the present tense in front of it into a plan.
andare — to go, and one of the irregular ones: vado (I) · vai (you) · va (he, she). Its plain form andare is what M5's sono andato was built from.

sentences.trap: English needs "will" or "going to" to mark a plan. Italian needs neither: the present plus domani says everything, and reaching for the future tense here writes the form Italians use least in conversation.
sentences.sound: do-MA-ni, stressed in the middle — no accent is written because the stress falls where the language expects it. VA-do is two short syllables.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to Milan
variations.changed: swap the destination — a stays in front of it

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm not going to Rome
variations.changed: non in front of the verb; the plan is cancelled, nothing else moves

variations.cue: Are you going to Rome tomorrow?
variations.changed: vado → vai, the time word to the end, and a question mark to ask

mistake.why: andare needs its a in front of a place: Domani vado a Roma. (The future tense, Domani andrò a Roma, is not wrong either — it is simply not what is said about an arrangement.)

sentences.usage: Any plan for tomorrow, in any company.
sentences.mnemonic: The time word carries the future, so the verb does not have to.

sentences.cue: Tonight I'm going out to eat

words.note: "This evening" — questa sera worn down into one word, the way stamattina and stanotte are. It covers the whole English "tonight" as long as you mean the evening rather than the small hours.

sentences.trap: The a in vado a mangiare is not the "to" of an infinitive — Italian infinitives need no "to". It is the same a as in vado a Roma: you are going somewhere in order to eat.
sentences.sound: sta-SE-ra, three syllables with the stress in the middle, and a single tapped r.

variations.cue: Tonight I'm going to study
variations.changed: swap what you are going to do — a stays in front of the plain verb

variations.display: Domani vado a mangiare con Anna
variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going out to eat with Anna
variations.changed: another time word, and con brings someone along

variations.cue: Tonight I'm not going out to eat
variations.changed: non in front of the whole thing, and the plan is off

mistake.why: andare needs its a before another verb: vado a mangiare. It is volere that takes the infinitive bare.

sentences.usage: Making an evening plan, or turning one down.
sentences.mnemonic: You GO somewhere to do it, so andare keeps its a.

words.note: prendere — to take, and an ordinary -ere verb: prendo (I) · prendi (you) · prende (he, she). It is also what you do with a coffee: prendo un caffè.
Masculine: il treno (one) · i treni (more than one). The e is close, so it is TRE-no and never "tray-no".

sentences.trap: English can say "I'm taking the train tomorrow" or "I'll take the train" and mean the same thing. Italian has one sentence for both, and it is the plain present.
sentences.sound: PREN-do, and TRE-no with a single tapped r. Neither e is the long "ay" of English — both are short and close.

variations.display: Domani prendo un caffè con Anna
variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm having a coffee with Anna
variations.changed: the same verb, doing what English does with "have"

variations.cue: Are you taking the train tomorrow?
variations.changed: -o → -i, the time word to the end, and a question mark

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm not taking the train
variations.changed: non in front of the verb; the object stays where it was

mistake.why: A particular train keeps its article: prendo il treno. Italian drops an article far less often than English does.

sentences.usage: Saying how you will get somewhere.
sentences.mnemonic: prendere takes trains and coffees alike.

sentences.display: La settimana prossima vado a Milano
sentences.cue: Next week I'm going to Milan
sentences.literal: The week next I-go to Milan

words.note: "Next week", and every piece of it is doing work English does differently: the article is compulsory, and prossima FOLLOWS the noun and agrees with it. The masculine partner is il mese prossimo.
Italian spells its own cities: Milano, Roma, Firenze, Venezia. A city takes a with no article — a Milano, a Roma.

sentences.trap: English says "next week" with two words and no article. Italian needs three, in the other order, with the adjective agreeing: la settimana prossima.
sentences.sound: set-ti-MA-na with the double t held, and PROS-si-ma with a doubled s. mi-LA-no is stressed in the middle.

variations.display: Il mese prossimo vado a Milano
variations.cue: Next month I'm going to Milan
variations.changed: a masculine noun, so the adjective goes masculine with it — prossimo

variations.display: Vado a Milano la settimana prossima
variations.cue: I'm going to Milan next week
variations.changed: the time phrase moved to the end, still with no preposition

variations.cue: Next week I'm not working
variations.changed: another verb behind the same time phrase, with non in front of it

mistake.why: The article is not optional and the adjective goes behind: La settimana prossima vado a Milano.

sentences.mnemonic: The week comes first and next comes after: la settimana prossima.

words.note: vedere — to see, and an ordinary -ere verb: vedo (I) · vedi (you) · vede (he, she). Meeting someone by arrangement is vedere in Italian, exactly as it is "see" in English.

sentences.trap: Italian puts no preposition in front of a person here. Spanish would (veo a mi hermana); Italian says vedo Anna, and the a would turn it into a destination.
sentences.sound: VE-do, both syllables short, with a close e.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm seeing Rohan
variations.changed: swap who you are meeting — nothing stands in front of the name

variations.cue: Are you seeing Anna tomorrow?
variations.changed: -o → -i, the time word to the end, and a question mark

variations.cue: Next week I'm seeing Anna
variations.changed: a longer time phrase in front, and the plan holds

mistake.why: No a in front of a person: Domani vedo Anna. The a of vado a Roma marks a destination, not an object.

sentences.mnemonic: vedere sees people straight, with nothing in between.

words.note: uscire — to go out, and its stem bends: esco (I) · esci (you) · esce (he, she). One word where English needs two, covering leaving the house for the evening as well as simply stepping outside.

sentences.trap: English builds "go out" from two words and can split them ("go straight out"). Italian has one verb, and non goes in front of the whole of it.
sentences.sound: ES-ko. sc before o is a hard "sk"; the same letters before i or e would be the sh of "ship", which is why esci is E-shee.

variations.cue: Tonight I'm going out
variations.changed: drop non and the evening is on again

variations.cue: Are you going out tonight?
variations.changed: esco → esci — and the sc changes sound with the vowel behind it

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm not going out
variations.changed: swap the time word; the refusal is the same shape

mistake.why: Drop the io — esco already says who. It comes back only to draw a contrast: Io non esco, ma Anna sì.

sentences.usage: Turning down an evening, or announcing one.
sentences.mnemonic: uscire keeps its u only in the plain form; the present starts with e.

words.note: fare — one verb for both "do" and "make", and its stem bends hard: faccio (I) · fai (you) · fa (he, she). It also does the weather — fa caldo, fa freddo — which M9 comes back to.

sentences.trap: English needs "are" and "-ing" to ask about a plan, and Italian needs neither: the plain present plus a time word is the whole question.
sentences.sound: FAI is one syllable — the a and the i glide together, like the English word "fie".

variations.cue: What are you doing tonight?
variations.changed: swap the time word — the question is otherwise identical

variations.display: Che cosa fai la settimana prossima?
variations.cue: What are you doing next week?
variations.changed: a longer time phrase, still with no preposition in front of it

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to Rome
variations.changed: the answer: a plan in the plain present

mistake.why: Drop the tu — fai already says who is being asked, and a pronoun here reads as a challenge rather than a question.

sentences.usage: The question that opens every arrangement.
sentences.mnemonic: fare does and makes, and it does the weather too.

words.note: partire — to leave, in the sense of setting off on a journey: parto (I) · parti (you) · parte (he, she). It is an -ire verb, and it is what a train does as well as what you do.

sentences.trap: partire is leaving FOR somewhere, not leaving something behind. "I'm leaving my bag" is a different verb (lasciare), which L1 does not need.
sentences.sound: PAR-to, one tapped r, and PRE-sto with a plain s before the t.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm leaving for Rome
variations.changed: per marks what you are setting off towards

variations.cue: Are you leaving tomorrow?
variations.changed: -o → -i and a question mark; nothing else is added

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm not leaving early
variations.changed: non in front of the verb, and presto still hugs it

mistake.why: Setting off towards a place takes per: parto per Roma. a belongs to andare — vado a Roma.

sentences.mnemonic: You PART from here and go per there.

sentences.display: Il mese prossimo vado a Milano
sentences.cue: Next month I'm going to Milan
sentences.literal: The month next I-go to Milan

words.note: "Next month", built exactly like la settimana prossima and differing only in gender: mese is masculine, so the article is il and the adjective is prossimo.

sentences.trap: The two time phrases look interchangeable and are not: la settimana prossima is feminine throughout, il mese prossimo masculine throughout. Mixing them is the commonest slip.
sentences.sound: ME-ze — the single s between two vowels again, said as a z through much of the north. PROS-si-mo has a doubled s that is held.

variations.cue: Next month I'm not working
variations.changed: another verb behind the same phrase, with non in front of it

variations.display: Vado a Milano il mese prossimo
variations.cue: I'm going to Milan next month
variations.changed: the time phrase to the end — no preposition either way

variations.display: La settimana prossima vado a Roma
variations.cue: Next week I'm going to Rome
variations.changed: the feminine partner, agreeing all the way through

mistake.display: Il mese prossima vado a Milano
mistake.why: mese is masculine, so the adjective is prossimo. The pair moves together: il mese prossimo, la settimana prossima.

sentences.usage: The longer plan, and the one people ask about at the end of a conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: The article and the adjective agree at both ends of the phrase.

sentences.display: Domani vado a comprare un regalo
sentences.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to buy a present
sentences.literal: Tomorrow I-go to buy a present

words.note: Masculine: un regalo (one) · i regali (more than one). It is the thing, not the act — giving one is fare un regalo.

sentences.trap: English "I'm going to buy" is a pure future marker with no journey in it. Italian's vado a comprare still means you are going somewhere to do it — and it is the ordinary way to say this anyway.
sentences.sound: re-GA-lo, stressed in the middle, with a tapped r and clear vowels throughout.

variations.display: Domani vado a comprare il pane
variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to buy the bread
variations.changed: swap what you are buying; the frame holds

variations.cue: Are you going to buy a present?
variations.changed: vado → vai and a question mark, with the a untouched

variations.display: Stasera vado a comprare un regalo
variations.cue: Tonight I'm going to buy a present
variations.changed: another time word in front — the plan moves with it

mistake.why: andare keeps its a in front of the second verb: vado a comprare.

sentences.usage: The errand you are announcing rather than the one you are already on.
sentences.mnemonic: andare always brings its a along.
